Which tuple orders mix?

Let N=2nN=2^n, let TT be the group of XOR translations, and let G=⟨T,P⟩G=\langle T,P\rangle. Each round applies the same fixed PP after a fresh shared uniform translation. An order tt mixes when the output of every distinct ordered tt-tuple converges to the uniform distribution on such tuples. Throughout, a tuple order and the number of rounds are separate parameters.

An exact test for all tuple orders

Write HH for the normal closure of TT in GG. Equivalently, HH is generated by all PjTP−jP^jTP^{-j}, for integer jj. The project’s block-of-rounds argument shows that order tt mixes exactly when HH acts transitively on distinct ordered tt-tuples. Hornauer, Stephan and Wernsdorf already used normal fixed-length round groups and double transitivity to study periodicity. Their Corollary 2 proves pairwise convergence for a Markov cipher whose round functions generate the alternating or symmetric group. Hornauer, Stephan and Wernsdorf, §2

Given a truth table, the full sequence of yes/no answers is computable in time polynomial in NN, even if tt is part of the input. Furst, Hopcroft and Luks gave polynomial-time permutation-group algorithms, including normal closure. Apply them to the nn basis translations and PP. Compute a point-stabilizer chain for HH. While the successive orbit lengths are N,N−1,N−2,…N,N-1,N-2,\ldots, each additional tuple entry can be sent to any remaining point while fixing the preceding ones. The first short orbit determines the first failing order. If one unused point remains, its image is forced, so (N−1)(N-1)-transitivity gives NN-transitivity. This decision avoids the N(N−1)⋯(N−t+1)N(N-1)\cdots(N-t+1) tuple state space. Finding round-by-round distances is a separate computation. Furst–Hopcroft–Luks, FOCS 1980

The accompanying group classifier builds HH from successive conjugate layers and exact Schreier–Sims membership tests. If one layer adds no generator, PP conjugates the generated finite subgroup into itself and therefore normalizes it. The subgroup already contains TT, so it is the required normal closure. Each strict extension at least doubles the order. At most log2(N!)\log_2(N!) strict extensions occur, irrespective of the order of PP. The optional SymPy dependency is pinned in the script. SymPy group operations

The four-wise threshold

For n≥3n\ge3, the following are equivalent.

  1. The walk mixes on ordered quadruples.
  2. GG contains the alternating group ANA_N.
  3. The walk mixes simultaneously on every tuple order 1≤t≤N−21\le t\le N-2.

Every nonidentity translation swaps N/2N/2 disjoint pairs. This is an even number for n≥2n\ge2, so H≤ANH\le A_N. If GG contains ANA_N, then HH is a nontrivial normal subgroup of the simple group ANA_N, hence H=ANH=A_N. An even permutation can realize any specified mapping on at most N−2N-2 points because two unused images allow its parity to be chosen. Conversely, a four-transitive HH of this degree must contain ANA_N by the classification of finite four-transitive groups. The proper exceptional groups have degrees 11, 12, 23 and 24. No power of two occurs. At orders N−1N-1 and NN, specifying the ordered images determines the permutation, whose parity at round rr is sign(P)r\mathrm{sign}(P)^r. Its total variation distance from uniform is then at least 1/21/2. For n=1n=1 the two translations already constitute S2S_2, and for n=2n=2 every permutation is affine and H=TH=T. Cameron, Theorem 1 and classification commentary

This is a corollary of the classification and the fixed-key-schedule group criterion. It implies a threshold for eventual convergence. The numbers of rounds needed for different tuple orders may still differ substantially.

An explicit separation at orders two and three

Identify the bits with m≥3m\ge3 field coordinates over F=𝔽2bF=\mathbb F_{2^b}. Thus n=bmn=bm. Use a cyclic coordinate rotation RR and the involution

Q(x)0=x0+x1x2,Q(x)i=xi(i≠0).Q(x)_0=x_0+x_1x_2,\qquad Q(x)_i=x_i\quad(i\ne0).

Set P=QRQP=QRQ. In coordinates relabeled by QQ, the translation normal closure is exactly ASL(m,F)\operatorname{ASL}(m,F), the affine transformations with determinant-one linear part. Here is a direct proof.

  • In these coordinates the round group is generated by RR and QTQQTQ. Conjugating a translation with vector uu by QQ adds uu and changes coordinate zero by u1x2+u2x1+u1u2u_1x_2+u_2x_1+u_1u_2. All these maps are affine with determinant one. The rotation also has determinant one in characteristic two.
  • Translations along coordinate zero commute with QQ. Their conjugates under RR give all coordinate translations in the normal closure. Conjugating translation by se2s e_2 with QQ gives that translation followed by E01(s)E_{01}(s), which adds sx1s x_1 to x0x_0. Thus the normal closure contains E01(s)E_{01}(s) for each field scalar ss.
  • Rotating yields the transvections along every adjacent pair around the coordinate cycle. For distinct indices their commutators give [Eij(s),Ejk(1)]=Eik(s)[E_{ij}(s),E_{jk}(1)]=E_{ik}(s), up to the immaterial sign in characteristic two. Following a simple path around the cycle gives every Eij(s)E_{ij}(s). Elementary row operations generate SL(m,F)\operatorname{SL}(m,F). Along with the translations, this proves equality.

Over 𝔽2\mathbb F_2, any two distinct nonzero vectors are linearly independent, so, after translating the first point to zero, any ordered pair of remaining differences can be sent to any other. This gives triple mixing. Four distinct points with XOR sum zero stay affinely dependent in the QQ coordinates, while affinely independent quadruples also exist. The largest mixing order is three.

For b>1b>1, SL(m,F)\operatorname{SL}(m,F) acts transitively on nonzero vectors, giving pair mixing. There are now both collinear and noncollinear triples. Collinearity survives every round in the QQ coordinates, so the largest mixing order is two. The construction uses an established hidden affine structure. The explicit cyclic construction and normal-closure computation are project derivations whose priority remains unverified. Brunetta–Calderini–Sala on hidden sums · Caranti–Dalla Volta–Sala on regular subgroups of affine groups

A fast published certificate and a four-bit sample

A transitive group of degree NN containing a cycle of prime length N/2<p<N−2N/2<p<N-2 in the cycle decomposition of one element must contain ANA_N. Indeed no nontrivial block system can admit this prime divisor, since the block size and the number of blocks are at most N/2N/2. A power of the element isolates the pp-cycle, and Jordan’s theorem applies to the resulting primitive group. As TT is transitive, the classifier checks up to sixteen actual round maps PτkP\tau_k for this certificate. Success proves all orders through N−2N-2 in one pass per key. Failure to find a certificate goes to the exact group algorithm. Unger describes stronger cycle-type certificates and proves that his Jordan and primitivity tests succeed on almost every uniform permutation as the degree grows. His sample-from-a-group bounds assume access to sufficiently random group elements. Unger, Theorems 1, 9–11

In the existing seeded four-bit sample of 10,000 tables, the classifier gave maximum order 14 for 9,974 and 1 for 26. The classic long-prime-cycle certificate accounted for 9,437 of the 9,974 successes. The remaining 563 decisions used stabilizer chains. In particular, every observed pairwise mixer also mixed on fourteen distinct inputs. The table in the preceding section supplies a four-bit permutation with maximum order three that this sample missed. The following command reproduces the audit from the repository root.

uv run --with sympy==1.14.0 python - <<'PY'
import csv
from collections import Counter
from group_mixing import group_profile

tallies = Counter()
with open("results/four_bit/samples.csv") as samples:
    for row in csv.DictReader(samples):
        result = group_profile(map(int, row["permutation"].split()))
        t = result["mixes_through"]
        assert (t >= 2) == (row["status"] == "mixing")
        tallies[t, "cycle_witness" in result] += 1
print(tallies)
PY

Which algorithmic guarantees transfer?

  • Polynomial in table size, including variable tuple order. Normal closure and stabilizer orbits give this bound without sampling. The implementation does not promise near-linear running time on every table. Furst–Hopcroft–Luks
  • Near-linear under a small-base hypothesis. Babai, Cooperman, Finkelstein and Seress analyze Monte Carlo order and membership algorithms for small-base groups. The natural action of ANA_N needs N−2N-2 base points, so this hypothesis cannot support a uniform near-linear bound here. Babai et al., ISSAC 1991
  • Orbit sampling with a group-element oracle. Lemmas 2.3–2.4 of the large-base reduction algorithm use nearly uniform independent group elements to sample point-stabilizer orbits. The cost explicitly includes generating such elements. A supplied PP table gives evaluations and actual generators. A universal cost bound for generating near-uniform elements of its translation normal closure would require another argument. Large-base reduction, §2.2
  • Primitivity tests. Beals gives nearly linear bounds for broad classes when testing for block systems, with stated alternating-socle exceptions. A primitive group can still have several pair orbits. Primitivity alone does not settle the pairwise decision. Beals, 2025 preprint
  • Typical random tables. Łuczak–Pyber show that almost every permutation lies in no transitive groups except the two giants. Babai–Hayes address directly the group obtained by adjoining a random permutation to a fixed group. Eberhard–Ford–Koukoulopoulos sharpen estimates on permutations belonging to some proper transitive subgroup. These results already imply that one repeated uniform PP almost surely gives every order through N−2N-2 in the large-degree limit. Unger makes cycle-structure recognition constructive. None of those typical-input statements bounds the miss probability on each individual mixing table. Łuczak–Pyber · Babai–Hayes · Eberhard–Ford–Koukoulopoulos

The references above establish several earlier routes to the same qualitative decision. This review found no theorem among them giving the notebook’s full near-linear, one-sided pairwise guarantee from one fixed explicit table without extra hypotheses. That leaves the priority of the particular Walsh-transform algorithm unverified.
